questions.q: A step up transformer is connected to an ac mains supply of 220 V to operate at $11000 \mathrm{~V}, 88$ watt. The current in the secondary circuit, ignoring the power loss in the transformer, is
questions.solution:
In secondary circuit, $P=V i$
$\Rightarrow 88=11000 i$
$\Rightarrow \quad i=\frac{88}{11 \times 10^3}=8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}$
$\Rightarrow \quad i=8 \mathrm{~mA}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The amplitude of the charge oscillating in a circuit decreases exponentially as $Q=Q_0 e^{-R t 2 L}$, where $Q_0$ is the charge at $t=0 \mathrm{~s}$. The time at which charge amplitude decreases to $0.50 Q_0$ is nearly:
[Given that $R=1.5 \Omega, L=12 \mathrm{mH}, \ln (2)=0.693$ ]
questions.solution:
Given $Q=Q_0 e^{-R t / 2 L}$
$R=1.5 \Omega, L=12 \mathrm{mH}, \operatorname{In}(2)=0.693$
$Q=0.5 Q_0, t=$ ?
$0.5 Q_0=Q_0 e^{-R t / 2 L}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2}=e^{-R t / 2 L}$
Taking log on both sides
$\ln \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\ln e^{-R t / 2 L}$
$\Rightarrow \ln 2=\frac{R t}{2 L}$
$t=\frac{2 L \operatorname{In} 2}{R}=\frac{2 \times 12 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.693}{1.5}$
$t=11.09 \mathrm{~ms}$

questions.q: An ac circuit contains a resistance of $1$ k$\Omega$, a capacitor of $0.1\ \mu F$ and an inductor of $1$ mH connected in series. The resonance frequency of the circuit is approximately :
questions.solution:
Given $L = 1 \text{ mH} = 10^{-3} \text{ H}$ and $C = 0.1\ \mu\text{F} = 10^{-7} \text{ F}$.

The resonance frequency of a series RLC circuit is given by $f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

Substituting the values:

$f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-3} \times 10^{-7}}}$

$f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-10}}}$

$f_r = \dfrac{10^5}{2\pi} \text{ Hz}$

$f_r = \dfrac{50}{\pi} \text{ kHz} \approx 15.9 \text{ kHz}$

Answer: $15.9$ kHz

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The peak value of an alternating current is $5$ A and frequency is $60$ Hz. How long will the current, starting from zero, take to reach the peak value ?
questions.solution:
The alternating current is given by $I = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$.

The time taken to reach the peak value from zero corresponds to a phase angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$2 \pi f t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$t = \dfrac{1}{4f}$

Given $f = 60$ Hz, we get:

$t = \dfrac{1}{4 \times 60} = \dfrac{1}{240}$ s.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{240}$ s

questions.q: In a series$LCR$ circuit, the inductance$L$ is $10mH$, capacitance $C$ is $1\mu F$ and resistance $R$ is $100Ω$. The frequency at which resonance occurs is:
questions.solution:
Resonance occurs when the value of inductive and capacitive reactances have equal magnitude but a phase difference of $180 °$.

Therefore, resonance frequency $= \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{\left(10 \times {10}^{- 3}\right) \times \left(1 \times {10}^{- 6}\right)}} = 1 . 591 \times {10}^{3} \approx 1 . 59kHz$

For DC circuits, $\omega=0 \begin{aligned}
X_{\mathrm{L}} & =\omega \mathrm{L} \\
\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}} & =0 \\
\mathrm{X}_2 & =0
\end{aligned}$
Hence $\quad X_2=0$

questions.q: The net impedance of circuit (as shown in figure) will be:
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the inductive impedance of the circuit is given by

${X}_{L} = \omegaL . . . \left(1\right)$

The formula to calculate the capacitive impedance of the circuit is given by

${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omegaC} . . . \left(2\right)$

The formula to calculate the total impedance of the circuit can be written as

$\begin{cases}Z & = & \sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{c} - {X}_{L}\right)}^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{1}{\omegaC} - \omegaL\right)}^{2}} . . . \left(3\right)\end{cases}$

Substitute the values of the given parameters into equation (3) to calculate the required net impedance of the circuit.

$\begin{cases}Z & = & \sqrt{{\left(10Ω\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50Hz \times \dfrac{{10}^{3}}{\pi} \times {10}^{- 6}F} - 2\pi \times 50Hz \times \dfrac{50}{\pi} \times {10}^{- 3}H\right)}^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{100 + 25}Ω \\ & = & \sqrt{125}Ω \\ & = & 5\sqrt{5}Ω\end{cases}$

questions.q:
An ac voltage $V=220\sin(2\times10^3 t)$ Volt is applied to a series LCR circuit. Then the current amplitude in this circuit is :
(Given : $L=10$ mH, $C=25\,\mu$F, $R=100\,\Omega$)
questions.solution:
Given $V = 220 \sin(2 \times 10^3 t)$ V, the peak voltage is $V_m = 220$ V and the angular frequency is $\omega = 2 \times 10^3$ rad/s.

The inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L = (2 \times 10^3) \times (10 \times 10^{-3}) = 20 \, \Omega$.

The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{(2 \times 10^3) \times (25 \times 10^{-6})} = \dfrac{1}{50 \times 10^{-3}} = 20 \, \Omega$.

Since $X_L = X_C$, the circuit is in resonance. The impedance of the circuit is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = R = 100 \, \Omega$.

The current amplitude is $I_m = \dfrac{V_m}{Z} = \dfrac{220}{100} = 2.2$ A.

Answer: $2.2$ A

questions.q: Which of the following combinations should be selected for better tuning of an LCR circuit used for communication?
questions.solution:
Quality factor is defined at resonance, when, inductive reactance is equal to the capacitive reactance.

It is defined as the ratio of voltage across the inductor or the capacitor and applied voltage or voltage across the resistor.

At resonance, impedance is equal to pure resistance, then, applied voltage and current are in phase.

Hence, the current is maximum.

$Q = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$.

$Q$ factor should be high.

questions.q:
A series$LCR$  circuit is connected to an ac voltage source.
When $L$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
If instead $C$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is:
questions.solution:
As phase angle contribution by capacitor and inductor are equal in magnitude, so
\begin{gathered}$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}$}=$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}$}$\\
\Rightarrow $\omega $\mathrm{L}=\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}$}
\end{gathered}$
It means that the RLC circuit is in resonance condition.
So, impedance at resonance, \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+\left(X_L-X_C\right)^2}=\sqrt{R^2+\left(X_L-X_L\right)^2}=\sqrt{R^2}=R\)
Thus, power factor, \(\cos \phi=\frac{R}{Z}=\frac{R}{R}=1\)$

questions.q: A series $L - C - R$ circuit containing $5 . 0H$ inductor, $80\muF$ capacitor and $40Ω$ resistor is connected to $230V$ variable frequency ac source. The angular frequencies of the source at which power transferred to the circuit is half the power at the resonant angular frequency are likely to be:
questions.solution:
$L = 5H, C = 80\muF, R = 40\omega; V = 230V$

Resonance angular frequency $= {\omega}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5 \times \left(80 \times {10}^{- 6}\right)}} = 50rad{s}^{- 1}$

Half power angular frequency $= {\omega}_{0} \pm \dfrac{R}{2L} = 50 \pm \dfrac{40}{2 \times 5} = 50 \pm 4 = 54\text{or}46$

We get,

${\omega}_{1} = 46rad{s}^{- 1}$

And ${\omega}_{2} = 54rad{s}^{- 1}$

questions.q: Power dissipated in an $L-C-R$ series circuit connected to an AC source of emf $\varepsilon$ is
questions.solution:
The emf of an LCR circuit is \(\varepsilon\).
The impedance of a series LCR circuit is given as,
\(Z=\sqrt{\left[R^2+\left(\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2\right]}\)
The power factor in a series LCR circuit is given as,
\(\cos \phi=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{|\mathrm{Z}|}\)
The power dissipated in the circuit is given as,
\(\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos \phi \\
& =\varepsilon \times \frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathrm{Z}|} \times \frac{\mathrm{R}}{|\mathrm{Z}|} \\
& =\frac{\varepsilon^2 \mathrm{R}}{\left[\mathrm{R}^2+\left(\omega \mathrm{L}-\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}}\right)^2\right]}
\end{aligned}\)
Thus, the power dissipated in the series \(L C R\) circuit is \(\frac{\varepsilon^2 R}{\left[R^2+\left(\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2\right]}\).

In an $A C$ circuit the emf (e) and the current (i) at any instant are given respectively by $e=E_0 \sin \omega t$ $i=I_0 \sin (\omega t-\phi)$
The average power in the circuit over one cycle of AC is
questions.solution:
Key Idea: The power is defined as the rate at which work is being done in the circuit.
Power $=$ rate of work done in one complete cycle.
$\begin{aligned}
& P_{a \nu}=\frac{W}{T} \\
& P_{a \nu}=\frac{\left(E_0 I_0 \cos \phi\right) T / 2}{T} \\
& P_{a \nu}=\frac{E_0 I_0 \cos \phi}{2}
\end{aligned}$
where $\cos \phi$ is called the power factor of an AC circuit.

questions.q: In an electrical circuit $R, L, C$ and an $\mathrm{AC}$ voltage source are all connected in series. When $L$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between the voltage and the current in the circuit is $\pi / 3$. If instead, $C$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\pi / 3$. The power factor of the circuit is
questions.solution:
Here, phase difference
$\begin{aligned}
\tan \phi & =\frac{X_L-X_C}{R} \\
\tan \frac{\pi}{3} & =\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}
\end{aligned}$
When, $L$ is removed
$\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{3}=\frac{X_C}{R} \\
& X_C=\sqrt{3} R
\end{aligned}$
When $C$ is removed
$\begin{gathered}
\tan \frac{\pi}{3}=\sqrt{3}=\frac{X_L}{R} \\
X_L=R \sqrt{3}
\end{gathered}$
Hence, in resonant circuit
$\begin{aligned}
\tan \phi & =\frac{\sqrt{3} R-\sqrt{3} R}{R}=0 \\
\phi & =0
\end{aligned} \therefore$ Power factor $\cos \phi=1$
It is the condition of resonance therefore phase difference between voltage and current is zero and power factor is $\cos \phi=1$.

questions.q:
For a series $LCR$ circuit, $I$ vs $\omega$ curve is shown 

(a) To the left of ${\omega}_{r}$, the circuit is mainly capacitive.
(b) To the left of ${\omega}_{r}$, the circuit is mainly inductive.
(c) At ${\omega}_{r}$, impedance of the circuit is equal to the resistance of the circuit.
(d) At ${\omega}_{r}$, impedance of the circuit is $0$.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
questions.solution:
The impedance of an AC circuit is given by, $Z = \sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{C} - {X}_{L}\right)}^{2}}$.

For current to be maximum $Z$ should be minimum. The value of $Z$ will be minimum when ${X}_{C} - {X}_{L} = 0$. Therefore, the value of $Z = R$. Hence, statement C is correct and statement D is wrong.

To the left of ${\omega}_{r}$ i.e. when $\omega < {\omega}_{r}$, ${X}_{C} > {X}_{L}$. Therefore, the circuit is mainly capacitive. Hence, statement A is correct and statement B is wrong.

Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Maximum power is dissipated in a circuit containing an inductor, a capacitor and a resistor connected in series with an $AC$ source, when resonance occurs.

Statement II: Maximum power is dissipated in a circuit containing pure resistor due to zero phase difference between current and voltage.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Statement $I$ is false but Statement $II$ is true
Both Statement $I$ and Statement $II$ are true
Statement $I$ is true but Statement $II$ is false
Both Statement $I$ and Statement $II$ are false
questions.solution:
The formula for impedance is given by 

$Z = \sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{L} - {X}_{C}\right)}^{2}}$

At resonance, ${X}_{L} = {X}_{C}$. So, ${Z}_{min} = R$

Power will be maximum when impedance is minimum. Thus the maximum power occurs in a purely resistive circuit.

options: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is correct but Statement II is false
questions.solution:
When an a.c. voltage is applied in a series LCR circuit, the current is increased first, attains a maximum and then decreases.

The formula to calculate the power factor is given by

$cosϕ = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + \left({{X}_{L}}^{2} - {{X}_{C}}^{2}\right)}} . . . \left(1\right)$

At resonance, ${X}_{L} = {X}_{C}$, Hence,

$cos{ϕ}_{resonance} = 1$

Thus, both the statements are true.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements :
Statement-I: The reactance of an ac circuit is zero. It is possible that the circuit contains a capacitor and an inductor.
Statement-II: In ac circuit, the average power delivered by the source never becomes zero.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
questions.solution:
The reactance of a circuit containing a capacitor and an inductor is given by $X = {X}_{L} - {X}_{C} = \omegaL - \dfrac{1}{\omegaC}$. An AC circuit has zero reactance at resonance, i.e., when, ${X}_{L} = {X}_{C}$. So, first statement is true.

The power consumption in an AC circuit is zero when circuit contains only inductance or capacitance since average power consumed in a cycle is zero for inductance or capacitance. So, second statement is false.

Given below are two statements:

Statement I : An AC circuit undergoes electrical resonance if it contains either a capacitor or an inductor.

Statement II: An AC circuit containing a pure capacitor or a pure inductor consumes high power due to its non-zero power factor. In the light of above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Statement I is false but statement II is true
Statement I is true but statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
questions.solution:
For resonance to occur the condition is ${X}_{L} = {X}_{C}$.

So, both inductor and capacitor is required.

The power factor is given by $cosϕ$.

For an inductor the power factor is zero-lagging, $cos90 ° = 0$. The angle between the voltage and current is $90 °$.

For a capacitor the power factor is zero-leading.

Hence, both statements are false.

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Smaller the band width, sharper the resonance and easier it is to tune an LCR circuit.
Reason (R) : Resonant frequency is arithmetic mean of half power frequencies.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) states that a smaller bandwidth leads to sharper resonance and easier tuning of an LCR circuit, which is true. A smaller bandwidth means a sharper peak in the resonance curve.
Reason (R) claims that the resonant frequency is the arithmetic mean of half-power frequencies, which is also true. However, this does not directly explain why a smaller bandwidth results in sharper resonance.
Thus, while both statements are true, the reason does not effectively explain the assertion. Therefore, the correct choice is:
(2) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Average power consumed in an ac circuit is equal to average power consumed by resistors in the circuit.
Reason (R) : Average power consumed by capacitor and inductor is zero
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A): Average power consumed in an AC circuit is equal to average power consumed by resistors in the circuit.
- This statement is true. In an AC circuit, only the resistive components consume average power. Capacitors and inductors do not consume power; they only store and release energy.
Reason (R): Average power consumed by the capacitor and inductor is zero.
- This statement is also true. Capacitors and inductors exchange energy with the circuit but do not dissipate power as heat; therefore, their average power consumption over a complete cycle is zero.
Now, assessing the relationship between the two statements:
- Both statements are true, and (R) correctly explains (A) because the zero average power of capacitors and inductors means that the average power in the circuit is indeed equal to that consumed by resistors.
Thus, the correct choice is:
(1) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

(c) at resonance the voltage across L and current in C differ in phase by \(180^{{}^{\circ}}\)

(a) Voltage across resistor, inductor and capacitor are \(50 $\mathrm{~V},$86.6 $\mathrm{~V}$\) and 206.6 V, respectively (b) Voltage across resistor, inductor and capacitor are \(10 $\mathrm{~V},$90 $\mathrm{~V}$\) and 30 V, respectively (c) Power factor of the circuit is \($\frac{5}{13}$\) (d) The circuit is capacitive in nature
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& V_1=\sqrt{V_R^2+V_L^2}=100 \quad \ldots (1) \\
& V_C-V_L=120 \quad \ldots (2) \\

& V_L=50 \sqrt{3} V=86.6 \mathrm{~V} ~\&~ V_C=206.6 \mathrm{~V} \\
& \cos \phi=\frac{V_R}{130}=\frac{5}{13}
\end{aligned}\)$

(b) fL
(c) \(1 / $\mathrm{fC}$\)
(d) \($\mathrm{L}$/ $\mathrm{f}$\)

\(\tau=\mathrm{RC} \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\frac{\tau}{\mathrm{C}}\)
\(\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{b} ~\&~ \mathrm{c}\) are correct.

questions.q:
A series LCR circuit is connected to a $45sin ( \omegat )$ Volt source. The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is ${10}^{5}rad{s}^{- 1}$ and current amplitude at resonance is ${I}_{0}$. When the angular frequency of the source is $\omega = 8 \times {10}^{4}rad{s}^{- 1}$, the current amplitude in the circuit is $0 . 05{I}_{0}$. If $L = 50mH$, match each entry in List-$I$ with an appropriate value from List-$II$ and choose the correct option.

  List-$I$   List-$II$
$P$ ${I}_{0}$ in $mA$ $1$ $44 . 4$
$Q$ The quality factor of the circuit $2$ $18$
$R$ The bandwidth of the circuit in $rad{s}^{- 1}$ $3$ $400$
$S$ The peak power dissipated at resonance in Watt $4$ $2250$
    $5$ $500$
questions.solution:
Resonant angular frequency is given by, $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = {10}^{5}$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(50 \times {10}^{- 3}\right)C}} = {10}^{5} ⇒ C = 2 \times {10}^{- 9}F$

Given: $V = 45sin\left(\omegat\right)$. Therefore, ${V}_{0} = 45$.

Now, ${I}_{0} = \dfrac{{V}_{0}}{R} = \dfrac{45}{R} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Inductive reactance, ${X}_{L} = \omegaL = \left(8 \times {10}^{4}\right) \times \left(50 \times {10}^{- 3}\right) = 4000Ω$.

and capacitive reactance, ${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omegaC} = \dfrac{1}{\left(8 \times {10}^{4}\right) \times \left(2 \times {10}^{- 9}\right)} = 6250Ω$.

For new current amplitude, we can write

questions.q:
When an inductor of inductance \($\frac{6}{\pi} \mathrm{H}$\), a capacitor of capacitance \($\frac{50}{\pi} \mu \mathrm{F}$\) and resistor of resistance \(R\) are connected in series with an AC supply of rms voltage \(220 $\mathrm{~V}$\) and frequency \(50 $\mathrm{~Hz}$\), the rms current through the circuit is \(440 $\mathrm{~mA}$\). Match the inductive reactance, \(X_L\) the capacitive reactance, \(X_C\) the resistance \(R\) and the impedance \(Z\) of the circuit given in List-I with the corresponding values given in List-II. \(
List- IList- II
(A)X_L(i)200 \Omega
(B)X_C(ii)300 \Omega
(C)R(iii)500 \Omega
(D)Z(iv)600 \Omega
\)
questions.solution:
Given, inductance of inductor, \(L=\frac{6}{\pi} \mathrm{H}\), 
capacitance of capacitor, \(C=\frac{50}{\pi} \mu \mathrm{F}\) 
supply voltage, \(V_{\text{rms }}=220 \mathrm{ V}\), 
supply frequency, \(f=50 \mathrm{ Hz}\) 
and supply current, \(I_{\mathrm{rms}}=440 \mathrm{ mA}\) 
Now, (A) inductive reactance, \(X_L=\omega L\)
$\begin{aligned}
X_L & =2 \pi f \times L \quad(\because \omega=2 \pi f) \\
& =2 \pi \times 50 \times \frac{6}{\pi}=600 \Omega \\
X_L & =600 \Omega
\end{aligned}\)
(B) Capacitance reactance, \(X_C=\frac{1}{\omega C}=\frac{1}{2 \pi f C}\)
$\begin{aligned}
X_C & =$\frac{\pi \times 10^6}{2 \pi \times 50 \times 50}$ \\
\Rightarrow \quad X_C & =$\frac{10^6}{2500 \times 2}$\Rightarrow X_C=200 \Omega
\end{aligned}\)
(C) Resistance, \(R\)
\(\therefore\) Impedance$ of $LCR circuit, \(Z^2=R^2+\left(X_L-X_C\right)^2\)
Putting the given values, we get$\begin{aligned}
(500)^2 & =R^2+(600-200)^2 \\
250000 & =R^2+(400)^2 \\
R^2 & =250000-160000 \\
R^2 & =90000 \Rightarrow R=300 \Omega
\end{aligned}\)
(D) Impedance,
\(Z=\frac{V_{\text{rms }}}{I_{\text{rms }}}=\frac{220}{440} \times 10^3 \Rightarrow Z=500 \Omega\)$

questions.solution:
(A) An AC generator works on the electromagnetic induction principle. So, $\left(A\right) \to II$

- (p): Current lags voltage by \(\pi / 2\).
4. (d) In purely resistive AC circuit -
(s): Current and voltage are in phase.
So the correct matching is:
(1) a-q, b-r, c-p, d-s

The correct matching is:

questions.q: The instantaneous current from an AC source is given by the equation $i = 14.14 \sin(100 \pi t)$, where $i$ is in amperes and $t$ is in seconds. What is the RMS value of the current?
questions.solution:
The standard equation for an alternating current is $i = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, where $I_0$ is the peak current.

Comparing the given equation $i = 14.14 \sin(100 \pi t)$ with the standard form, we find the peak current to be:
$I_0 = 14.14\text{ A}$

The RMS value of the current ($I_{rms}$) is related to the peak current by the formula:
$I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$

Using the approximation $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$, we get:
$I_{rms} = \dfrac{14.14}{1.414} = 10\text{ A}$

Therefore, the RMS value of the current is $10\text{ A}$.

Answer: $10\text{ A}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The frequency at which the current amplitude is maximum in a series LCR circuit is independent of the resistance of the circuit.
Reason (R): The maximum current amplitude at resonance in a series LCR circuit is inversely proportional to the resistance of the circuit.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: The current amplitude in a series LCR circuit is maximum at resonance. The resonant frequency is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$, which depends only on the inductance and capacitance, and is independent of the resistance.

Reason (R) is true: At resonance, the inductive reactance and capacitive reactance cancel each other ($X_L = X_C$), making the impedance minimum and equal to the resistance ($Z = R$). The maximum current amplitude is $I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{R}$, which is inversely proportional to the resistance.

However, Reason (R) does not explain Assertion (A). The correct explanation for Assertion (A) is that the condition for resonance ($X_L = X_C$) does not involve resistance. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

An alternating current is given by the equation $I = I_0 \sin(120\pi t)$. Match the instantaneous values of the current in List-I with the shortest time taken to reach them starting from $t = 0$ in List-II.

List-IList-II

(B) RMS value(ii) $\dfrac{1}{240}$ s
(C) Half of peak value(iii) $\dfrac{1}{480}$ s
(D) First return to zero(iv) $\dfrac{1}{720}$ s

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

The given current equation is $I = I_0 \sin(120\pi t)$.

Match List-I with List-II.

(A)Pure Inductor(I)Blocks DC completely in steady state
(B)Pure Capacitor(II)Offers zero opposition to DC
(C)Pure Resistor(III)Impedance is purely resistive and minimum
(D)Series LCR circuit at resonance(IV)Opposition to alternating current is independent of frequency

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
(A) Pure Inductor: The inductive reactance is $X_L = 2\pi f L$. For direct current (DC), the frequency $f = 0$, so $X_L = 0$. It offers zero opposition to DC. Matches with (II).

(B) Pure Capacitor: The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$. For DC, $f = 0$, so $X_C = \infty$. It blocks DC completely in steady state. Matches with (I).

(C) Pure Resistor: The resistance $R$ of a pure resistor does not depend on the frequency of the alternating current. Matches with (IV).

(D) Series LCR circuit at resonance: At resonance, the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance ($X_L = X_C$), making the total impedance $Z = R$. The impedance is purely resistive and is at its minimum value. Matches with (III).

The correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

questions.q:
Match the electrical behaviors described in List-I with the corresponding circuit combinations in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Allows steady DC, AC current lags the applied voltage(I) Pure Resistor
(B) Blocks steady DC, AC current leads the applied voltage(II) Series LR circuit
(C) Allows steady DC, AC current is in phase with the applied voltage(III) Series RC circuit
(D) Blocks steady DC, AC current lags the applied voltage(IV) Series LCR circuit with $X_L > X_C$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
A pure resistor allows steady DC to flow, and in an AC circuit, the current and voltage are in phase. This matches (C) with (I).

A series LR circuit allows steady DC to flow (since an inductor has zero reactance for DC), but in an AC circuit, the inductive reactance causes the current to lag the voltage. This matches (A) with (II).

A series RC circuit blocks steady DC because the capacitor acts as an open circuit. In an AC circuit, the capacitive reactance causes the current to lead the voltage. This matches (B) with (III).

A series LCR circuit blocks steady DC due to the presence of the capacitor. When $X_L > X_C$, the net reactance is inductive, causing the AC current to lag the voltage. This matches (D) with (IV).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A light bulb connected in series with an ideal inductor glows brighter when connected to a DC source than when connected to an AC source of the same rms voltage.
Reason (R): The inductive reactance of an ideal inductor is zero for direct current, leading to a lower total impedance in the circuit.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
For a DC source, the frequency $f = 0$, so the inductive reactance $X_L = 2\pi f L = 0$. The total impedance of the circuit is simply the resistance of the bulb ($Z = R$).

For an AC source, the frequency $f > 0$, so the inductor offers a non-zero reactance $X_L$. The total impedance of the circuit becomes $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$, which is greater than $R$.

Since the rms voltage is the same in both cases, the current drawn from the DC source ($I = \dfrac{V}{R}$) is greater than the rms current drawn from the AC source ($I_{rms} = \dfrac{V}{Z}$).

The brightness of the bulb depends on the power dissipated ($P = I^2 R$). Since the current is higher for the DC source, the bulb glows brighter.

Therefore, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The standard household alternating current (AC) supply in India is rated at $220\text{ V}$. What is the peak voltage of this supply?
questions.solution:
The voltage rating given for an AC supply always represents its root mean square (RMS) value. Therefore, the RMS voltage is $V_{rms} = 220\text{ V}$.

The relationship between the peak voltage ($V_0$) and the RMS voltage for a sinusoidal AC wave is given by:
$V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times V_{rms}$

Substituting the given value:
$V_0 = 1.414 \times 220\text{ V} \approx 311\text{ V}$

Thus, the peak voltage of the supply is approximately $311\text{ V}$.

Answer: $311\text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The rms voltages across the components of a series LCR circuit are given below:
Resistor ($R$): $16\text{ V}$
Inductor ($L$): $24\text{ V}$
Capacitor ($C$): $12\text{ V}$

The instantaneous current flowing through the circuit is given by the equation $i(t) = 4\sqrt{2} \sin(100\pi t)\text{ A}$. The impedance of the circuit is:
questions.solution:
The rms voltage of the source is calculated using the phasor addition formula:

$V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$

$V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{16^2 + (24 - 12)^2} = \sqrt{256 + 144} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ V}$

The peak current from the given equation $i(t) = 4\sqrt{2} \sin(100\pi t)$ is $I_0 = 4\sqrt{2}\text{ A}$.

The rms current is:

$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 4\text{ A}$

The impedance of the circuit is:

$Z = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{I_{\text{rms}}} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5\ \Omega$

Answer: $5\ \Omega$

questions.q:
In a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source, the rms voltage drops across the resistor, inductor, and capacitor are $40 \text{ V}$, $100 \text{ V}$, and $70 \text{ V}$ respectively. If the resistance of the circuit is $20 \Omega$, what is the rms current in the circuit and the phase angle between the source voltage and the current?
(Take $\tan 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{4}$)
questions.solution:
The rms current $I_{\text{rms}}$ is the same through all components in a series circuit. We can find it directly using the voltage drop across the resistor and Ohm's law:
$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{V_R}{R} = \dfrac{40}{20} = 2 \text{ A}$

The phase angle $\phi$ between the source voltage and the current can be found using the voltage phasor diagram:
$\tan \phi = \dfrac{V_L - V_C}{V_R}$

Substitute the given rms voltage drops:
$\tan \phi = \dfrac{100 - 70}{40} = \dfrac{30}{40} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

Since $\tan 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, the phase angle is $\phi = 37^{\circ}$.

Answer: $2 \text{ A}$ and $37^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor of capacitance $C$ is connected to an AC source of constant peak voltage $V_m$ but variable angular frequency $\omega$. Which of the following correctly describes the graph of the peak displacement current ($I_d$) between the capacitor plates versus the angular frequency ($\omega$)?
options: A straight line passing through the origin
A straight line parallel to the angular frequency axis
questions.solution:
The peak displacement current between the plates of a capacitor is equal to the peak conduction current in the connecting wires.

$I_d = \dfrac{V_m}{X_C}$

Since the capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, substituting this gives:

$I_d = V_m (\omega C)$

For a constant peak voltage $V_m$ and constant capacitance $C$, the peak displacement current is directly proportional to the angular frequency ($I_d \propto \omega$).

Therefore, the graph of $I_d$ versus $\omega$ is a straight line passing through the origin.

A rectangular hyperbola would represent the variation of $X_C$ with $\omega$, while a horizontal line would incorrectly imply that the current is independent of frequency.

Answer: A straight line passing through the origin

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an AC circuit containing a single pure element, the variations of voltage $V$ and current $I$ with time $t$ are observed. At $t = 0$, the voltage is at its positive maximum value $V_0$, whereas the current is zero and is increasing in the positive direction. If the peak value of the current is $I_0$, identify the circuit element and the correct expression for its reactance.
questions.solution:
From the given description, the voltage is at its positive maximum at $t = 0$, which corresponds to a cosine function: $V = V_0 \cos \omega t = V_0 \sin(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2})$.

The current is zero at $t = 0$ and increasing positively, which corresponds to a sine function: $I = I_0 \sin \omega t$.

Comparing the phases, the voltage leads the current by a phase angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ($90^{\circ}$). This is the characteristic of a purely inductive circuit.

The reactance of any pure circuit element is defined as the ratio of the peak voltage to the peak current, so $X_L = \dfrac{V_0}{I_0}$.

Answer: Pure inductor with reactance $\dfrac{V_0}{I_0}$

questions.q: A series $LCR$ circuit with inductance $L = 50\ \text{mH}$, capacitance $C = 20\ \mu\text{F}$, and resistance $R = 40\ \Omega$ is connected to a variable frequency AC source of $200\ \text{V}$ (rms). What is the angular frequency of the source at which the power dissipated in the circuit is maximum, and what is the value of this maximum power?
questions.solution:
Maximum power dissipation in a series $LCR$ circuit occurs at resonance, where the impedance is purely resistive and minimum ($Z = R$).

The resonant angular frequency is given by:
$\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$

Substituting the given values:
$\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{50 \times 10^{-3} \times 20 \times 10^{-6}}}$
$\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1000 \times 10^{-9}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-6}}} = 1000\ \text{rad}\ \text{s}^{-1}$

At resonance, the maximum power dissipated is:
$P_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R}$

Substituting the given values:
$P_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{(200)^2}{40} = \dfrac{40000}{40} = 1000\ \text{W}$

Answer: $1000\ \text{rad}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ and $1000\ \text{W}$

questions.q: Two series LCR circuits, Circuit 1 and Circuit 2, are connected to the same variable frequency AC source of peak voltage $V_0$. Circuit 1 has inductance $L$, capacitance $C$, and resistance $R$. Circuit 2 has inductance $2L$, capacitance $\dfrac{C}{2}$, and resistance $2R$. If $f_1$ and $f_2$ are their respective resonant frequencies, and $I_1$ and $I_2$ are their respective maximum peak currents at resonance, which of the following relationships is correct?
questions.solution:
The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

For Circuit 1: $f_1 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$

For Circuit 2: $f_2 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(2L)\left(\dfrac{C}{2}\right)}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$

Thus, $f_1 = f_2$.

At resonance, the impedance of the circuit is minimum and equal to its resistance ($Z = R$). The maximum peak current is $I = \dfrac{V_0}{R}$.

For Circuit 1: $I_1 = \dfrac{V_0}{R}$

For Circuit 2: $I_2 = \dfrac{V_0}{2R} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{V_0}{R}\right) = \dfrac{I_1}{2}$

Thus, $I_1 = 2I_2$.

Answer: $f_1 = f_2$ and $I_1 = 2I_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An air-filled parallel plate capacitor is connected to an AC source of constant voltage amplitude, resulting in a peak displacement current $I_0$ between its plates. If the frequency of the AC source is halved and simultaneously a dielectric slab of dielectric constant $K = 2$ is inserted to completely fill the space between the capacitor plates, what will be the new peak displacement current?
questions.solution:
The initial peak displacement current is equal to the peak conduction current:

$I_0 = \dfrac{V_m}{X_C} = V_m (2\pi f) C$

When the frequency is halved, the new frequency is $f' = \dfrac{f}{2}$.

When a dielectric of $K = 2$ is completely inserted, the new capacitance becomes $C' = 2C$.

The new peak displacement current is:

$I' = V_m (2\pi f') C' = V_m \left(2\pi \dfrac{f}{2}\right) (2C)$

$I' = V_m (2\pi f) C = I_0$

Thus, the decrease in frequency is exactly compensated by the increase in capacitance, and the displacement current remains unchanged.

Answer: $I_0$
questions.question: An air-filled parallel plate capacitor is connected to an AC source of constant voltage amplitude, resulting in a peak displacement current $I_0$ between its plates. If the frequency of the AC source is halved and simultaneously a dielectric slab of dielectric constant $K = 2$ is inserted to completely fill the space between the capacitor plates, what will be the new peak displacement current?
questions.explanation:
The initial peak displacement current is equal to the peak conduction current:

$I_0 = \dfrac{V_m}{X_C} = V_m (2\pi f) C$

When the frequency is halved, the new frequency is $f' = \dfrac{f}{2}$.

When a dielectric of $K = 2$ is completely inserted, the new capacitance becomes $C' = 2C$.

The new peak displacement current is:

$I' = V_m (2\pi f') C' = V_m \left(2\pi \dfrac{f}{2}\right) (2C)$

$I' = V_m (2\pi f) C = I_0$

Thus, the decrease in frequency is exactly compensated by the increase in capacitance, and the displacement current remains unchanged.

Answer: $I_0$

questions.q: The variation of rms current ($I_{rms}$) with angular frequency ($\omega$) for a series LCR circuit is plotted. The resulting curve shows that the current reaches its maximum peak value at an angular frequency of $1000$ rad/s. If the capacitance in the circuit is $10\ \mu$F, what is the value of the inductance?
questions.solution:
The peak current in a series LCR circuit occurs at the condition of resonance.

From the described graph, the angular resonant frequency is $\omega_r = 1000$ rad/s.

The condition for resonance in terms of angular frequency is $\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.

Squaring both sides and rearranging for inductance $L$ gives:

$L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_r^2 C}$

Given $C = 10\ \mu\text{F} = 10 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F} = 10^{-5} \text{ F}$.

Substituting the values:

$L = \dfrac{1}{(1000)^2 \times 10^{-5}}$

$L = \dfrac{1}{10^6 \times 10^{-5}} = \dfrac{1}{10} \text{ H}$

$L = 0.1 \text{ H} = 100 \text{ mH}$

Answer: $100$ mH

questions.q:
An AC voltage $V = 250 \sin(100 t)$ V is applied to a series LCR circuit containing a resistor of $R = 60 \, \Omega$, an inductor of $L = 1.2$ H, and a capacitor of $C = 250 \, \mu$F. Match the quantities in List-I with their corresponding values in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Inductive reactance(I) $40 \, \Omega$
(B) Capacitive reactance(II) $2.5$ A
(C) Impedance(III) $100 \, \Omega$
(D) Current amplitude(IV) $120 \, \Omega$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
From the given voltage equation $V = 250 \sin(100 t)$ V, the peak voltage is $V_m = 250$ V and the angular frequency is $\omega = 100$ rad/s.

The inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L = 100 \times 1.2 = 120 \, \Omega$. This matches (A) with (IV).

The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{100 \times 250 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{25000 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{0.025} = 40 \, \Omega$. This matches (B) with (I).

The impedance of the series LCR circuit is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + (120 - 40)^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + 80^2} = 100 \, \Omega$. This matches (C) with (III).

The current amplitude is $I_m = \dfrac{V_m}{Z} = \dfrac{250}{100} = 2.5$ A. This matches (D) with (II).

The correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)

questions.q: In a series LCR circuit, the impedance is $10\ \Omega$ and the rms current flowing through it is $5\text{ A}$. The rms voltages across the resistor and the inductor are $30\text{ V}$ and $50\text{ V}$, respectively. If the voltage across the capacitor is greater than the voltage across the inductor, the rms voltage across the capacitor is:
questions.solution:
The rms voltage of the source is given by Ohm's law for the entire circuit:

$V_{\text{rms}} = Z \times I_{\text{rms}} = 10 \times 5 = 50\text{ V}$

Using the phasor addition formula for voltages in a series LCR circuit:

$V_{\text{rms}}^2 = V_R^2 + (V_C - V_L)^2$

Substituting the known values:

$50^2 = 30^2 + (V_C - 50)^2$

$2500 = 900 + (V_C - 50)^2$

$(V_C - 50)^2 = 1600$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$V_C - 50 = \pm 40$

This gives two possible values for $V_C$:
$V_C = 50 + 40 = 90\text{ V}$
or
$V_C = 50 - 40 = 10\text{ V}$

Since it is given that the voltage across the capacitor is greater than the voltage across the inductor ($V_C > V_L$, i.e., $V_C > 50\text{ V}$), we select $V_C = 90\text{ V}$.

Answer: $90\text{ V}$

questions.q: In a series LCR circuit, the resistance is $8\ \Omega$, the inductive reactance is $10\ \Omega$, and the net impedance of the circuit is $10\ \Omega$. If the alternating current in the circuit leads the applied voltage, what is the value of the capacitive reactance?
questions.solution:
The net impedance $Z$ of a series LCR circuit is given by:

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}$

Given $Z = 10\ \Omega$, $R = 8\ \Omega$, and $X_L = 10\ \Omega$, we can substitute these values into the equation:

$10 = \sqrt{8^2 + (X_C - 10)^2}$

Squaring both sides:

$100 = 64 + (X_C - 10)^2$

$(X_C - 10)^2 = 36$

$X_C - 10 = \pm 6$

This gives two possible values for $X_C$:
$X_C = 10 + 6 = 16\ \Omega$
or
$X_C = 10 - 6 = 4\ \Omega$

The problem states that the alternating current leads the applied voltage, which means the circuit is capacitive in nature. For a capacitive circuit, the capacitive reactance must be greater than the inductive reactance ($X_C > X_L$).

Since $X_L = 10\ \Omega$, we must have $X_C > 10\ \Omega$. Therefore, the correct value is $X_C = 16\ \Omega$.

Answer: $16\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A purely capacitive circuit with capacitance $C$ is connected to an ac source. If the alternating current flowing in the circuit is given by $I = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the instantaneous voltage $V_C$ across the capacitor is
questions.solution:
In a purely capacitive circuit, the voltage lags behind the current by a phase angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Given the current $I = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the voltage can be expressed as:
$V_C = V_0 \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

The peak voltage $V_0$ is related to the peak current $I_0$ by the capacitive reactance $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$:
$V_0 = I_0 X_C = \dfrac{I_0}{\omega C}$

Substituting $V_0$ into the voltage expression:
$V_C = \dfrac{I_0}{\omega C} \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin(\theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2}) = -\cos(\theta)$, we get:
$V_C = -\dfrac{I_0}{\omega C} \cos(\omega t)$

Answer: $-\dfrac{I_0}{\omega C} \cos(\omega t)$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In an oscillating LCR circuit with small resistance, the amplitude of the oscillating charge decreases exponentially with time.

Reason (R): The resistor in the circuit continuously dissipates electromagnetic energy as heat, causing the total energy to decrease exponentially as $E = E_0 e^{-Rt/L}$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct: In a damped LCR circuit, the presence of resistance causes the amplitude of the oscillating charge to decay exponentially as $Q = Q_0 e^{-\dfrac{Rt}{2L}}$.

Reason (R) is correct: The resistor continuously dissipates the stored electromagnetic energy in the form of Joule heating. As a result, the total energy of the circuit decreases exponentially with time according to $E = E_0 e^{-\dfrac{Rt}{L}}$.

Furthermore, (R) is the correct explanation of (A) because the exponential decay of the charge amplitude is a direct physical consequence of the continuous dissipation of the total electromagnetic energy in the circuit.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Assertion (A): In a series LCR circuit with $L = 0.1\text{ H}$ and $C = 10\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ connected to an AC source $V = 200 \sin(1000t)$, the power factor is unity.
Reason (R): The linear frequency ($\nu$) of the AC source is $1000\text{ Hz}$, which is equal to the resonant frequency ($\nu_0$) of the circuit.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
For the given AC source $V = 200 \sin(1000t)$, the angular frequency is $\omega = 1000\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is:
$\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.1 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}}} = 1000\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Since $\omega = \omega_0$, the circuit is at resonance and the power factor is unity ($\cos\phi = 1$). Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

The linear frequency of the source is $\nu = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{1000}{2\pi} = \dfrac{500}{\pi}\text{ Hz}$.
The value $1000$ refers to the angular frequency, not the linear frequency. Thus, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false.

(B) Mean Voltage over half cycle(II) Zero

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a damped $LCR$ circuit, the time required for the charge amplitude to decrease to half of its initial value is $t_1$. The time required for the maximum total electrical energy of the circuit to decrease to half of its initial value is $t_2$. The ratio $t_1 : t_2$ is:
questions.solution:
The charge amplitude in a damped $LCR$ circuit decays exponentially as:
$Q = Q_0 e^{-\dfrac{Rt}{2L}}$

For the amplitude to drop to half ($Q = \dfrac{Q_0}{2}$):
$\dfrac{1}{2} = e^{-\dfrac{R t_1}{2L}} \Rightarrow t_1 = \dfrac{2L}{R} \ln(2)$

The total electrical energy $U$ is proportional to the square of the charge amplitude ($U \propto Q^2$), so it decays as:
$U = U_0 e^{-\dfrac{Rt}{L}}$

For the energy to drop to half ($U = \dfrac{U_0}{2}$):
$\dfrac{1}{2} = e^{-\dfrac{R t_2}{L}} \Rightarrow t_2 = \dfrac{L}{R} \ln(2)$

Taking the ratio of the two times:
$\dfrac{t_1}{t_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2L}{R} \ln(2)}{\dfrac{L}{R} \ln(2)} = 2$

Thus, the ratio $t_1 : t_2$ is $2 : 1$.

Answer: $2 : 1$

questions.q: An ideal inductor of inductance $L$ is connected across an alternating voltage source. If the instantaneous voltage is given by $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, what is the expression for the instantaneous current $I$ flowing through the circuit?
questions.solution:
In a purely inductive circuit, the current lags behind the voltage by a phase angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Given the voltage $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the phase of the current can be written as:
$I = I_0 \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

The peak current $I_0$ is related to the peak voltage $V_0$ by the inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$:
$I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{X_L} = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}$

Substituting $I_0$ into the current expression:
$I = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L} \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin(\theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2}) = -\cos(\theta)$, we get:
$I = -\dfrac{V_0}{\omega L} \cos(\omega t)$

Answer: $-\dfrac{V_0}{\omega L} \cos(\omega t)$

questions.q: A capacitor is connected to a $200\text{ V}$, $50\text{ Hz}$ AC source. If the peak value of the current in the circuit is $2\sqrt{2}\text{ A}$, the capacitance of the capacitor is:
questions.solution:
The rms current in the circuit is related to the peak current by:
$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\text{ A}$

The capacitive reactance $X_C$ is given by:
$X_C = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{I_{\text{rms}}} = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100\ \Omega$

We also know that $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$. Rearranging for capacitance $C$:
$C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f X_C}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 100} = \dfrac{1}{10000\pi}\text{ F}$

Converting to microfarads ($\mu\text{F}$):
$C = \dfrac{1}{10000\pi} \times 10^6\ \mu\text{F} = \dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \mu\text{F}$

Answer: $\dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \mu\text{F}$
questions.question: A capacitor is connected to a $200\text{ V}$, $50\text{ Hz}$ AC source. If the peak value of the current in the circuit is $2\sqrt{2}\text{ A}$, the capacitance of the capacitor is:
questions.explanation:
The rms current in the circuit is related to the peak current by:
$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\text{ A}$

The capacitive reactance $X_C$ is given by:
$X_C = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{I_{\text{rms}}} = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100\ \Omega$

We also know that $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$. Rearranging for capacitance $C$:
$C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f X_C}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 100} = \dfrac{1}{10000\pi}\text{ F}$

Converting to microfarads ($\mu\text{F}$):
$C = \dfrac{1}{10000\pi} \times 10^6\ \mu\text{F} = \dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \mu\text{F}$

Answer: $\dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \mu\text{F}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The RMS value of an alternating current is defined as the equivalent direct current that transfers the same amount of charge through a circuit in a half cycle.

Reason (R): For a sinusoidal alternating current, the peak value is $\sqrt{2}$ times the RMS value.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
The Assertion is false. The RMS (Root Mean Square) value of an alternating current is defined as the equivalent direct current that produces the same heating effect (power dissipation) in a given resistor over a complete cycle. The equivalent direct current that transfers the same amount of charge in a half cycle is defined as the mean (or average) value of the AC.

The Reason is true. For a sinusoidal alternating current $I = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the mathematical relationship between the peak value $I_0$ and the RMS value $I_{rms}$ is $I_0 = \sqrt{2} I_{rms}$.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.q: A plot of current amplitude versus angular frequency for a series $L-C-R$ circuit shows a peak at an angular frequency of $100 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. The two points on the curve where the current amplitude is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ times the peak value correspond to angular frequencies of $90 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$ and $110 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. If the circuit contains a $0.5 \text{ H}$ inductor, what is the resistance of the circuit?
questions.solution:
The bandwidth of the series $L-C-R$ circuit is the difference between the half-power angular frequencies.

Bandwidth $\Delta \omega = \omega_2 - \omega_1 = 110 - 90 = 20 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

The formula for bandwidth is $\Delta \omega = \dfrac{R}{L}$.

Substituting the given values:
$20 = \dfrac{R}{0.5}$

$R = 20 \times 0.5 = 10 \ \Omega$.

Answer: $10 \ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series LCR circuit is connected to an AC source $V = 100\sqrt{2} \sin(1000 t)$ Volts. The current amplitude in the circuit is $2$ A. Given that $R = 50 \, \Omega$, $L = 100$ mH, and the voltage leads the current, the value of capacitance $C$ is :
questions.solution:
From the given voltage equation $V = 100\sqrt{2} \sin(1000 t)$, the peak voltage is $V_m = 100\sqrt{2}$ V and the angular frequency is $\omega = 1000$ rad/s.

The impedance of the circuit is given by $Z = \dfrac{V_m}{I_m} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{2} = 50\sqrt{2} \, \Omega$.

Using the impedance formula $Z^2 = R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2$, we have:
$(50\sqrt{2})^2 = 50^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2$
$5000 = 2500 + (X_L - X_C)^2$
$(X_L - X_C)^2 = 2500 \implies |X_L - X_C| = 50 \, \Omega$

The inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L = 1000 \times (100 \times 10^{-3}) = 100 \, \Omega$.

Since the voltage leads the current, the circuit is inductive, which means $X_L > X_C$.
Therefore, $X_L - X_C = 50 \implies 100 - X_C = 50 \implies X_C = 50 \, \Omega$.

The capacitance is $C = \dfrac{1}{\omega X_C} = \dfrac{1}{1000 \times 50} = \dfrac{1}{50000} = 20 \times 10^{-6}$ F $= 20 \, \mu$F.

Answer: $20 \, \mu$F

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An unknown electrical device draws a steady current of $0.5 \text{ A}$ when connected to a $20 \text{ V}$ DC supply. When the same device is connected to a $20 \text{ V}$ AC supply, it draws an rms current of $0.4 \text{ A}$. The power factor of the device when connected to the AC supply is
questions.solution:
When connected to a DC supply, the steady current indicates the device does not contain a series capacitor. It offers only resistance $R$.
$R = \dfrac{V_{DC}}{I_{DC}} = \dfrac{20}{0.5} = 40 \ \Omega$

When connected to an AC supply, the device offers an impedance $Z$.
$Z = \dfrac{V_{AC}}{I_{AC}} = \dfrac{20}{0.4} = 50 \ \Omega$

The power factor of the device is the ratio of its resistance to its impedance:
$\cos \phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{40}{50} = 0.8$

Answer: $0.8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a series LCR circuit connected to an ac source, the rms voltages across the inductor, capacitor, and resistor are $80\text{ V}$, $20\text{ V}$, and $80\text{ V}$ respectively. If the peak current in the circuit is $5\sqrt{2}\text{ A}$, what are the power factor and the average power dissipated in the circuit?
questions.solution:
Given:
$V_L = 80\text{ V}$
$V_C = 20\text{ V}$
$V_R = 80\text{ V}$
Peak current, $I_0 = 5\sqrt{2}\text{ A}$

The rms voltage of the source is given by phasor addition:
$V_{rms} = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$
$V_{rms} = \sqrt{80^2 + (80 - 20)^2}$
$V_{rms} = \sqrt{6400 + 3600} = \sqrt{10000} = 100\text{ V}$

The rms current is:
$I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\text{ A}$

The power factor ($\cos\phi$) is:
$\cos\phi = \dfrac{V_R}{V_{rms}} = \dfrac{80}{100} = 0.8$

The average power dissipated in the circuit is:
$P = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$
$P = 100 \times 5 \times 0.8 = 400\text{ W}$
(Alternatively, $P = V_R I_{rms} = 80 \times 5 = 400\text{ W}$)

Answer: $0.8$, $400\text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ac source of $200 \text{ V}$ (rms) is connected across a series combination of a resistor of $30 \ \Omega$, an inductor of reactance $80 \ \Omega$, and a capacitor of reactance $40 \ \Omega$. The power dissipated in the circuit, and the additional capacitive reactance that must be connected in series to achieve maximum power dissipation are, respectively:
questions.solution:
The net impedance of the series LCR circuit is given by:
$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$
$Z = \sqrt{30^2 + (80 - 40)^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50 \ \Omega$

The rms current in the circuit is:
$I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{200}{50} = 4 \text{ A}$

The power dissipated in the circuit is:
$P = I_{rms}^2 R = (4)^2 \times 30 = 16 \times 30 = 480 \text{ W}$

For maximum power dissipation, the circuit must be in resonance, which requires the total capacitive reactance to equal the inductive reactance:
$X_{C(\text{total})} = X_L = 80 \ \Omega$

Since the existing capacitive reactance is $40 \ \Omega$, the additional capacitive reactance needed in series is:
$X_{C(\text{additional})} = 80 \ \Omega - 40 \ \Omega = 40 \ \Omega$

Answer: $480 \text{ W}$ and $40 \ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a series $L-C-R$ circuit, the average power dissipated is half of the maximum power at the frequencies where the phase angle between current and voltage is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Reason (R): At half-power frequencies, the numerical value of the net reactance of the circuit is equal to its resistance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
At half-power frequencies, the current amplitude is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ of its maximum value. This occurs when the impedance $Z = \sqrt{2}R$.

Since $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, we get $(X_L - X_C)^2 = R^2$, which implies $|X_L - X_C| = R$. Thus, the numerical value of the net reactance equals the resistance. Therefore, Reason (R) is true.

The phase angle $\phi$ is given by $\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$. Since $|X_L - X_C| = R$, we have $\tan \phi = \pm 1$, which gives $\phi = \pm \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

At this phase angle, the power factor is $\cos \phi = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, and the average power is half of the maximum power. Therefore, Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) provides the direct mathematical condition (net reactance equals resistance) that leads to the phase angle being $\pm \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Hence, Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.q: A pure inductor of inductance $\dfrac{2}{\pi}\text{ H}$ is connected to a $220\text{ V}$, $50\text{ Hz}$ AC supply. The rms value of the current in the circuit is:
questions.solution:
The inductive reactance of the circuit is given by $X_L = 2\pi f L$.

Substituting the given values:
$X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times \left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right) = 200\ \Omega$

According to Ohm's law for AC circuits, the rms current is:
$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{X_L}$

$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{220}{200} = 1.1\text{ A}$

Answer: $1.1\text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil draws a steady current of $2 \text{ A}$ when connected to a $100 \text{ V}$ d.c. source. When the same coil is connected to a $100 \text{ V}, 50 \text{ Hz}$ a.c. source, it draws an rms current of $1 \text{ A}$. The inductance of the coil is:
questions.solution:
For the DC source, the frequency is zero, so the inductive reactance $X_L = 0$. The coil acts as a pure resistor.
$R = \dfrac{V_{dc}}{I_{dc}} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50 \, \Omega$

For the AC source, the coil offers both resistance and inductive reactance. The total impedance $Z$ is:
$Z = \dfrac{V_{ac}}{I_{ac}} = \dfrac{100}{1} = 100 \, \Omega$

The impedance of an RL circuit is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.
$100 = \sqrt{50^2 + X_L^2}$
$10000 = 2500 + X_L^2$
$X_L^2 = 7500 \implies X_L = 50\sqrt{3} \, \Omega$

The inductive reactance is $X_L = 2\pi f L$.
$50\sqrt{3} = 2\pi \times 50 \times L$
$50\sqrt{3} = 100\pi L$
$L = \dfrac{50\sqrt{3}}{100\pi} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2\pi} \text{ H}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2\pi} \text{ H}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a series $L-C-R$ circuit, the resonant angular frequency is $500 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. The difference between the two angular frequencies at which the current amplitude is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ of its maximum value is $20 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. If the capacitance in the circuit is $40 \ \mu\text{F}$, what are the values of inductance and resistance respectively?
questions.solution:
The resonant angular frequency is given by $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.

Squaring both sides:
$\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{LC}$

Rearranging for $L$:
$L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0^2 C} = \dfrac{1}{(500)^2 \times 40 \times 10^{-6}}$
$L = \dfrac{1}{250000 \times 40 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{10} = 0.1 \text{ H}$

The difference between the half-power frequencies is the bandwidth, which is given by $\dfrac{R}{L}$.

$\text{Bandwidth} = \dfrac{R}{L} = 20 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Substituting the value of $L$:
$\dfrac{R}{0.1} = 20$

$R = 20 \times 0.1 = 2 \ \Omega$.

Answer: $0.1 \text{ H}$ and $2 \ \Omega$

$\text{Bandwidth} = \dfrac{R}{L} = 20 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Substituting the value of $L$:
$\dfrac{R}{0.1} = 20$

$R = 20 \times 0.1 = 2 \ \Omega$.

Answer: $0.1 \text{ H}$ and $2 \ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series LCR circuit with inductance $10 \text{ mH}$, capacitance $100 \text{ \mu F}$, and resistance $50 \text{ \Omega}$ is connected to an AC source of voltage $V = 100\sqrt{2} \sin(1000t)$ volt. The RMS current and the power factor of the circuit are respectively:
questions.solution:
From the given voltage equation $V = 100\sqrt{2} \sin(1000t)$, the peak voltage is $V_0 = 100\sqrt{2} \text{ V}$ and the angular frequency is $\omega = 1000 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

The RMS voltage is $V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} = 100 \text{ V}$.

The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is:

$\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10 \times 10^{-3} \times 100 \times 10^{-6}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-6}}} = 1000 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Since $\omega = \omega_0$, the circuit is in resonance. At resonance, the impedance $Z$ is equal to the resistance $R$ ($Z = 50 \text{ \Omega}$) and the phase difference between voltage and current is zero.

The power factor is $\cos \phi = \cos(0) = 1$.

The RMS current is $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{100}{50} = 2 \text{ A}$.

Answer: $2 \text{ A}, 1$

Since $\omega = \omega_0$, the circuit is in resonance. At resonance, the impedance $Z$ is equal to the resistance $R$ ($Z = 50 \text{ \Omega}$) and the phase difference between voltage and current is zero.

The power factor is $\cos \phi = \cos(0) = 1$.

The RMS current is $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{100}{50} = 2 \text{ A}$.

Answer: $2 \text{ A}, 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radio tuning circuit contains a series LCR combination. To tune into a station broadcasting at a frequency of $\dfrac{10^6}{2\pi}$ Hz, the circuit must resonate at this frequency. If the circuit has a fixed inductor of $100\ \mu$H, what should be the capacitance of the variable capacitor?
questions.solution:
The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit is given by $f_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

Squaring both sides and rearranging for capacitance $C$ gives:

$C = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2 f_r^2 L}$

Given $f_r = \dfrac{10^6}{2\pi}$ Hz and $L = 100\ \mu\text{H} = 10^{-4}$ H.

Substituting the values:

$C = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2 \left(\dfrac{10^6}{2\pi}\right)^2 \times 10^{-4}}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2 \left(\dfrac{10^{12}}{4\pi^2}\right) \times 10^{-4}}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{10^{12} \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{1}{10^8} \text{ F}$

$C = 10^{-8} \text{ F} = 10 \text{ nF}$

Answer: $10$ nF

questions.q: An alternating voltage given by the equation $V = V_0 \sin(100\pi t)$ is applied across a purely inductive circuit. What is the minimum time after $t = 0$ that the current in the circuit reaches its maximum positive value?
questions.solution:
In a purely inductive circuit, the current lags the voltage by a phase angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

Given the voltage equation $V = V_0 \sin(100\pi t)$, the current equation can be written as:
$I = I_0 \sin\left(100\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -I_0 \cos(100\pi t)$

For the current to reach its maximum positive value ($I = I_0$), we must have:
$-I_0 \cos(100\pi t) = I_0$
$\cos(100\pi t) = -1$

The smallest positive angle for which the cosine is $-1$ is $\pi$.
Therefore, $100\pi t = \pi$
$t = \dfrac{1}{100}$ s.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{100}$ s

questions.q: A series LCR circuit is connected to an AC source of variable frequency. At a particular frequency, the current in the circuit is in phase with the applied voltage. If the inductive reactance at this frequency is $50\ \Omega$ and the capacitance of the circuit is $20\ \mu\text{F}$, the frequency of the AC source is :
questions.solution:
The current is in phase with the voltage when the circuit is at resonance.

At resonance, the inductive reactance ($X_L$) equals the capacitive reactance ($X_C$):

$X_L = X_C$

Given $X_L = 50\ \Omega$, we have $X_C = 50\ \Omega$.

The capacitive reactance is given by $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.

Substituting the given values ($C = 20\ \mu\text{F} = 20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$):

$50 = \dfrac{1}{\omega \times 20 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\omega = \dfrac{1}{50 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{1000 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{10^{-3}} = 1000\text{ rad/s}$

The linear frequency $f$ is related to the angular frequency $\omega$ by $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$:

$f = \dfrac{1000}{2\pi} = \dfrac{500}{\pi}\text{ Hz}$

Answer: $\dfrac{500}{\pi}\text{ Hz}$

questions.q: A coil when connected across a steady DC voltage $V$ draws a current $I_0$. When it is connected across an AC source of the same rms voltage $V$ and frequency $f$, it draws an rms current of $\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$. If the frequency of the AC source is increased to $2f$ while keeping the rms voltage constant, what will be the new rms current drawn by the coil?
questions.solution:
When connected to a steady DC voltage $V$, the inductive reactance is zero. The resistance of the coil is $R = \dfrac{V}{I_0}$.

When connected to an AC source of frequency $f$, the impedance is $Z = \dfrac{V}{I_{rms}} = \dfrac{V}{\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}} = \sqrt{2}R$.

Since $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$, we have $\sqrt{2}R = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$, which gives $X_L = R$.

When the frequency is doubled to $2f$, the new inductive reactance becomes $X_L' = 2X_L = 2R$.

The new impedance is $Z' = \sqrt{R^2 + (2R)^2} = \sqrt{5}R$.

The new rms current drawn is $I' = \dfrac{V}{Z'} = \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{5}R} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{5}}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{5}}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion and the other is labelled as Reason.

Assertion: When an AC voltage $V = 260 \sin(500 t)$ V is applied to a series LCR circuit with $L = 160$ mH, $C = 10 \, \mu$F, and $R = 50 \, \Omega$, the peak current in the circuit is $2$ A.

Reason: In this circuit, the voltage leads the current because the inductive reactance is greater than the capacitive reactance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
questions.solution:
From the given equation $V = 260 \sin(500 t)$ V, we have $V_m = 260$ V and $\omega = 500$ rad/s.

The inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L = 500 \times 160 \times 10^{-3} = 80 \, \Omega$.

The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{500 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{5 \times 10^{-3}} = 200 \, \Omega$.

The impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{50^2 + (80 - 200)^2} = \sqrt{50^2 + (-120)^2} = 130 \, \Omega$.

The peak current is $I_m = \dfrac{V_m}{Z} = \dfrac{260}{130} = 2$ A. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

For the Reason: Since $X_C (200 \, \Omega) > X_L (80 \, \Omega)$, the circuit is predominantly capacitive. In a capacitive circuit, the current leads the voltage. The Reason incorrectly states that $X_L > X_C$ and that voltage leads current. Thus, the Reason is incorrect.

Therefore, the Assertion is correct but the Reason is incorrect.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.

questions.q:
An AC source of $200 \text{ V}$ (rms) is connected across a series LCR circuit. The rms current in the circuit is observed to be $4 \text{ A}$, and the voltage leads the current by a phase angle of $53^{\circ}$. If the capacitive reactance of the circuit is $10 \Omega$, what are the values of the resistance and the inductive reactance, respectively?
(Take $\cos 53^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$)
questions.solution:
The impedance of the circuit is given by:
$Z = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{I_{\text{rms}}} = \dfrac{200}{4} = 50 \Omega$

From the impedance triangle, the resistance $R$ is:
$R = Z \cos \phi = 50 \times \cos 53^{\circ} = 50 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 30 \Omega$

Since the voltage leads the current, the circuit is inductive ($X_L > X_C$). The net reactance is:
$X_L - X_C = Z \sin \phi = 50 \times \sin 53^{\circ} = 50 \times \dfrac{4}{5} = 40 \Omega$

Given that the capacitive reactance $X_C = 10 \Omega$:
$X_L - 10 = 40 \Rightarrow X_L = 50 \Omega$

Thus, the resistance is $30 \Omega$ and the inductive reactance is $50 \Omega$.

Answer: $30 \Omega$ and $50 \Omega$

questions.q:
Assertion: In a series LCR circuit, if the rms voltages across the inductor, capacitor, and resistor are $60\text{ V}$, $20\text{ V}$, and $30\text{ V}$ respectively, the peak voltage of the AC source is $50\sqrt{2}\text{ V}$.
Reason: The voltages across the inductor and capacitor are out of phase by $\pi$ radians, and their resultant is out of phase with the resistor's voltage by $\pi/2$ radians.
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion: The rms voltage of the source is found using phasor addition:
$V_{rms} = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$
$V_{rms} = \sqrt{30^2 + (60 - 20)^2} = \sqrt{900 + 1600} = 50\text{ V}$
The peak voltage of the source is $V_0 = V_{rms}\sqrt{2} = 50\sqrt{2}\text{ V}$. Thus, the Assertion is true.

Reason: In a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the inductor ($V_L$) leads the current by $\pi/2$, while the voltage across the capacitor ($V_C$) lags the current by $\pi/2$. Therefore, $V_L$ and $V_C$ are exactly $\pi$ radians ($180^\circ$) out of phase. Their resultant, $V_L - V_C$, is either leading or lagging the current by $\pi/2$. Since the voltage across the resistor ($V_R$) is in phase with the current, the resultant of the reactive components is out of phase with $V_R$ by $\pi/2$ radians ($90^\circ$). This perpendicular phase relationship is the exact reason why the voltages are added vectorially using the Pythagorean theorem to find the source voltage. Thus, the Reason is true and correctly explains the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source, decreasing the capacitance will always result in a decrease in the rms current.
Reason (R): Decreasing the capacitance increases the capacitive reactance, which decreases the net impedance if the circuit is initially inductive ($X_L > X_C$).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
The capacitive reactance is given by $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$. When the capacitance $C$ is decreased, the capacitive reactance $X_C$ increases.

The net impedance of a series LCR circuit is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

If the circuit is initially inductive ($X_L > X_C$), an increase in $X_C$ will reduce the magnitude of the difference $(X_L - X_C)$. This causes the net impedance $Z$ to decrease.

Since the rms current is $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z}$, a decrease in the impedance $Z$ leads to an increase in the rms current. Therefore, decreasing the capacitance can actually increase the current, making Assertion (A) false.

Reason (R) correctly states that decreasing capacitance increases capacitive reactance, which in turn decreases the net impedance if $X_L > X_C$. Thus, Reason (R) is true.

Answer: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a series LCR circuit, if the inductive reactance is twice the capacitive reactance ($X_L = 2X_C$) and the resistance equals the capacitive reactance ($R = X_C$), the current lags the source voltage by $45^{\circ}$.
Reason (R): The rms current in a series LCR circuit is maximum when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
For the Assertion (A):
The phase angle $\phi$ in a series LCR circuit is given by:
$\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$
Substituting the given values ($X_L = 2X_C$ and $R = X_C$):
$\tan \phi = \dfrac{2X_C - X_C}{X_C} = \dfrac{X_C}{X_C} = 1$
$\phi = 45^{\circ}$
Since $X_L > X_C$, the circuit is net inductive. In an inductive circuit, the voltage leads the current, meaning the current lags the source voltage by $45^{\circ}$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

For the Reason (R):
The rms current in a series LCR circuit is $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}}$. This current is maximum when $X_L = X_C$ (resonance condition). Thus, Reason (R) is true.

However, the resonance condition does not explain the $45^{\circ}$ phase lag in the specific non-resonant case described in the assertion. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

Since $X_L > X_C$, the circuit is net inductive. In an inductive circuit, the voltage leads the current, meaning the current lags the source voltage by $45^{\circ}$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

For the Reason (R):
The rms current in a series LCR circuit is $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}}$. This current is maximum when $X_L = X_C$ (resonance condition). Thus, Reason (R) is true.

However, the resonance condition does not explain the $45^{\circ}$ phase lag in the specific non-resonant case described in the assertion. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.q: An alternating voltage, starting from zero, takes $5$ ms to reach its maximum positive value. What is the frequency of the AC source?
questions.solution:
The time taken by an alternating voltage to reach its maximum value from zero is one-fourth of its total time period ($T$).

Therefore, $\dfrac{T}{4} = 5$ ms

$T = 20$ ms $= 20 \times 10^{-3}$ s

The frequency $f$ is the reciprocal of the time period:

$f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{20 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{1000}{20} = 50$ Hz.

Answer: $50$ Hz

questions.q: A series LCR circuit is connected to an AC source of rms voltage $130\ \text{V}$. The circuit components have a resistance of $12\ \Omega$, an inductive reactance of $14\ \Omega$, and a capacitive reactance of $9\ \Omega$. What will be the reading of an ideal AC voltmeter connected strictly across the series combination of the inductor and the capacitor?
questions.solution:
First, calculate the net impedance $Z$ of the series LCR circuit:

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$

Substitute the given values ($R = 12\ \Omega$, $X_L = 14\ \Omega$, $X_C = 9\ \Omega$):

$Z = \sqrt{12^2 + (14 - 9)^2}$
$Z = \sqrt{144 + 5^2}$
$Z = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13\ \Omega$

Next, find the rms current $I_{\text{rms}}$ flowing through the circuit using Ohm's law for AC circuits:

$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \dfrac{130\ \text{V}}{13\ \Omega} = 10\ \text{A}$

An ideal AC voltmeter connected across the inductor and capacitor combination will measure the net rms voltage across them. The net reactance of the LC combination is:

$X_{\text{LC}} = |X_L - X_C| = |14 - 9| = 5\ \Omega$

The voltage reading $V_{\text{LC}}$ across this combination is:

$V_{\text{LC}} = I_{\text{rms}} \times X_{\text{LC}} = 10\ \text{A} \times 5\ \Omega = 50\ \text{V}$

Answer: $50\ \text{V}$

questions.q: Two ideal capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected to two different AC sources. The first circuit has capacitance $C_1 = C$, rms voltage $V_1 = V$, and frequency $f_1 = f$. The second circuit has capacitance $C_2 = \dfrac{C}{2}$, rms voltage $V_2 = 2V$, and frequency $f_2 = 2f$. The ratio of the rms currents $I_1 : I_2$ in the two circuits is:
questions.solution:
The rms current in a purely capacitive circuit is given by $I = \dfrac{V}{X_C}$.

Since $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$, the current can be written as $I = V(2\pi f C)$.

For the first circuit:
$I_1 = V(2\pi f C)$

For the second circuit:
$I_2 = (2V)(2\pi \cdot 2f \cdot \dfrac{C}{2}) = 2V(2\pi f C) = 2I_1$

Therefore, the ratio of the rms currents is $I_1 : I_2 = 1 : 2$.

Answer: $1 : 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a damped oscillating LCR circuit, the amplitude of the oscillating charge at $t=0$ is $Q_0$. If the charge amplitude at time $t_0$ is $Q_1$ and at time $2t_0$ is $Q_2$, which of the following algebraic relationships is correct?
questions.solution:
In a damped LCR circuit, the amplitude of the oscillating charge decays exponentially with time according to the relation:
$Q(t) = Q_0 e^{-\dfrac{Rt}{2L}}$

At time $t = t_0$, the amplitude is:
$Q_1 = Q_0 e^{-\dfrac{Rt_0}{2L}}$
$\Rightarrow e^{-\dfrac{Rt_0}{2L}} = \dfrac{Q_1}{Q_0}$

At time $t = 2t_0$, the amplitude is:
$Q_2 = Q_0 e^{-\dfrac{R(2t_0)}{2L}} = Q_0 \left(e^{-\dfrac{Rt_0}{2L}}\right)^2$

Substituting the value of the exponential term:
$Q_2 = Q_0 \left(\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_0}\right)^2 = \dfrac{Q_1^2}{Q_0}$

Rearranging the equation, we get:
$Q_1^2 = Q_0 Q_2$

This shows that the charge amplitudes at equally spaced time intervals form a geometric progression.

Answer: $Q_1^2 = Q_0 Q_2$
